title: Faster, cheaper, safer? The G20 should address the tradeoffs in cross-border payments.
gist: The authors argue the G20's 2020 cross-border payments roadmap has never systematically confronted the fact that its five goals conflict — the FATF's 2025 expansion of the 'travel rule' to nearly all payments risks excluding the financially undocumented even as speed targets are already being exceeded, while AI-driven fraud is outrunning security controls that real-time payments make harder to enforce.

insights.claim: The G20's 2020 Roadmap for Enhancing Cross-Border Payments set quantitative targets for four of its five goals (faster, cheaper, more transparent, more inclusive) but never set a target for the fifth goal, safety and security, and has never systematically assessed whether the five goals are mutually compatible.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural design flaw in a major global payments policy initiative — the absence of a safety/security target and of tradeoff analysis — that could produce unintended regulatory conflicts as implementation deepens through 2027.
insights.quote: the roadmap process has lacked one critical element: a systematic assessment of whether its ambitious goals are mutually compatible, or whether progress toward one may come at the expense of another.

insights.claim: The FSB has itself acknowledged the G20 roadmap is not on track to meet its ambitious targets, stating more work is needed to convert international policy into real-world gains, while FSB Chair and Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in March that the process has not yet 'reached the point where we have to consider trade-offs' — a framing the authors argue is increasingly outdated.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The authors directly dispute the FSB chair's public position, arguing tradeoff conversations are already unavoidable — a signal that G20/FSB policy communications may lag the actual regulatory reality on the ground.
insights.quote: reached the point where we have to consider trade-offs

themes.theme: The revised travel rule: safety versus inclusion

insights.claim: In 2025, the FATF broadened the original post-9/11 'travel rule' from wire transfers to all payments and value transfers, including purchases of goods and services, and made previously optional personal data — an individual's address and birth date — mandatory to accompany payments.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A major, recent (2025) expansion of mandatory personal-data requirements across nearly all cross-border payment types — a compliance cost and data-collection burden increase for payment providers globally.
insights.quote: the FATF broadened the travel rule in principle to all payments and value transfers, including purchases of goods and services
insights.locator: The 'travel rule' as a test case section

insights.claim: The FATF's de minimis threshold for simplified travel-rule information ($1,000 or €1,000 maximum) was set two decades ago and remains unadjusted; a lack of consensus among FATF members means a uniform de minimis approach across countries remains highly unlikely, creating a patchwork that global banks have found difficult to navigate and have often responded to by simply not applying the exception at all for cross-border payments.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Banks defaulting to full information requirements rather than navigating the inconsistent de minimis patchwork means the intended inclusion-friendly exception is being effectively nullified in practice — a compliance-driven de facto tightening beyond what regulators intended.
insights.quote: This has created a patchwork that global banks have found difficult to navigate, leading them not to apply the exception for cross-border payments.

insights.claim: The G20's inclusion target is for more than 90 percent of individuals wishing to send or receive a remittance to be able to access cross-border electronic remittance services by end-2027, but the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025 found only 79 percent of adults globally, and 75 percent in low- and middle-income economies, have a financial account of any kind — a gap the stricter travel-rule information requirements risk widening further.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A quantified, dated (2027) inclusion target already faces an 11-to-15 percentage point account-ownership gap, and tightening documentation requirements is likely to make that gap harder rather than easier to close — a risk indicator for remittance-service providers targeting underbanked markets.

insights.claim: Stricter identity-verification requirements disproportionately risk excluding people who lack a birth certificate because they were born in areas without formal birth registration, particularly women and girls who face registration gaps — even though FATF allows substitute information (e.g., an approximate birth date or village name), institutions tend to err on the side of caution and reject it.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Even where regulatory flexibility exists on paper (substitute information), institutional risk-aversion in practice can still exclude the intended beneficiaries — implying real-world financial inclusion outcomes may lag the formal rule text considerably.
insights.locator: A tradeoff between safety and inclusion section

themes.theme: Speed versus security under AI-driven fraud

insights.claim: The G20's 2021 speed target — 75 percent of retail cross-border payments available to recipients within one hour by end-2027 — has already effectively been achieved ahead of schedule: the FSB reported in 2026 that 75 percent of payments now reach beneficiary banks within just ten minutes, with many arriving in seconds.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The speed goal is essentially solved years ahead of its 2027 deadline, meaning payments infrastructure has structurally shifted toward near-instant settlement — a background condition that is now colliding with unresolved fraud and AML screening capacity.
insights.quote: 75% of payments reach beneficiary banks in just 10 minutes, with many arriving in seconds.
insights.locator: Faster, better, but still secure section

insights.claim: Real-time and instant payments leave little time for sanctions and crime-combating screening controls to operate before funds move, forcing some institutions toward after-the-fact (e.g., daily rather than real-time) screening — a tension the FATF's own draft guidance acknowledges.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Instant-payment infrastructure structurally weakens pre-transaction AML/sanctions screening, a systemic vulnerability that criminal and sanctioned actors could exploit as real-time payments become the global default.

insights.claim: The UK responded to this exact tension in 2024 by giving banks new powers to delay payments for up to seventy-two hours to allow time for crime controls and intervention where necessary.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A concrete national policy precedent (UK's 72-hour delay power) that other G20 jurisdictions may adopt as a template for reconciling speed and security goals — worth watching for replication elsewhere.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The UK recognized this tension"

insights.claim: According to the OECD, 69 percent of reporting jurisdictions experienced an increase in payments fraud and scams between 2024 and 2025, and Interpol found AI is linked to more than half of all cybercrime in Africa, where financial, data, and law enforcement authorities often lack adequate capacity to respond.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
entities: Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the AI-fraud surge (69% of jurisdictions reporting increases; >50% of African cybercrime AI-linked) — a rising structural cost and capacity strain for payment providers and regulators, particularly in lower-resource markets.
insights.quote: AI is linked to more than half of all cybercrime in Africa
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "AI is adding to the challenge"

insights.claim: Tim Adams, CEO of the Institute of International Finance, warned at the FSB Cross-border Payment Summit in March 2026 that 'growing payments fraud requires security to retake a prominent place in the agenda,' reflecting industry-level concern that the roadmap's speed and cost priorities have crowded out security focus.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A named industry leader's explicit call to rebalance the G20 payments agenda toward security is a signal that institutional pressure for a policy course-correction is already building.
insights.quote: growing payments fraud requires security to retake a prominent place in the agenda

insights.claim: The authors call on the G20 to task the FSB with identifying, assessing, and transparently communicating where the roadmap's targets conflict, examining how tradeoffs differ across markets and jurisdictions, and determining which compromises are acceptable versus unacceptable, rather than continuing to focus solely on implementation of all five goals simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable governance recommendation — formal tradeoff analysis by the FSB — that would materially change how the G20 payments roadmap is implemented and evaluated going into its 2027 deadline.

top_entities: Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development
